questions.stem: In psychology, adaptive behaviour is behaviour that:
options: helps a person cope with the demands of everyday life
is shown by most people in a population at a particular time
has been changed by a person to fit a new social situation
occurs automatically without any conscious thought or effort
questions.explanation: Adaptive behaviour allows a person to function effectively, look after themselves and get along with others. Behaviour shown by most people is the statistical idea of normality, and common behaviour is not always adaptive.

questions.stem: Noah is so worried about germs that he has stopped catching public transport and now misses most of his university classes. His behaviour is best described as:
options: adaptive, because it lowers his anxiety each time he avoids a bus or train
maladaptive, because it interferes with his daily functioning
adaptive, because avoiding germs protects his physical health over time
maladaptive, because it is statistically rare in people of his age group
questions.explanation: Maladaptive behaviour is counterproductive: it stops a person meeting the demands of daily life, as Noah's avoidance stops him studying. The short-term relief from avoidance does not make it adaptive, because it maintains the fear and costs him his studies.

questions.stem: Which example is the clearest case of adaptive behaviour?
options: A student who is nervous about a speech practises it several times beforehand
A student who is nervous about a speech stays home sick on the day it is due
A student who is nervous about a speech stays up all night rewriting it again
A student who is nervous about a speech refuses to talk to classmates about it
questions.explanation: Practising channels the nervousness into preparation and improves performance, so it helps the student cope. Staying home avoids the speech but leaves the problem unsolved and the fear in place, which is maladaptive.

questions.stem: The statistical approach to normality judges behaviour as normal if it:
options: allows the person to function in daily life
suits the setting in which it occurs
is typical of most people in the population
conforms to the rules of the person's culture
questions.explanation: The statistical approach defines normal as what is common, for example within a set range around the average of a normal distribution. Conforming to the rules of a culture is the sociocultural approach.

questions.stem: A student argues that a person with an IQ of 140 should be classed as abnormal because so few people score that high. Which approach to normality is he using, and what is its main weakness?
options: Statistical; it labels desirable but rare traits as abnormal
Medical; it labels any rare trait as a symptom of an illness
Functional; it ignores whether the behaviour is common or rare
Sociocultural; it ignores how rare the trait is in the population
questions.explanation: The statistical approach treats rarity as abnormality, so it cannot tell desirable rare traits, such as very high intelligence, from undesirable ones. It also counts common problems, such as mild anxiety, as normal simply because they are common.

questions.stem: The sociocultural approach to normality judges behaviour as normal if it:
options: falls within two standard deviations of the population's average score
allows the person to look after themselves and keep a job or study
does not match the symptoms listed for a disorder in a diagnostic manual
fits the norms and expectations of the person's culture
questions.explanation: Social norms are the unwritten rules for how people are expected to behave in a group or culture, and the sociocultural approach treats conforming to them as normal. Its weakness is that norms differ between cultures, so the same behaviour can be normal in one and abnormal in another.

questions.stem: In some cultures it is polite to avoid direct eye contact with older people, while in others avoiding eye contact can be read as dishonest. This shows a limitation of which approach to normality?
options: Statistical
Medical
Functional
Sociocultural
questions.explanation: The sociocultural approach depends on the norms of a particular culture, so a judgement made by one culture's standards can wrongly label behaviour that is normal in another. The statistical and medical approaches do not rest on a culture's rules of conduct.

questions.stem: The functional approach to normality judges behaviour as abnormal when it:
options: occurs in a setting where most people would not behave that way
stops a person managing the everyday tasks of their life
breaks the unwritten rules that most people in the culture follow
would have been considered unusual in an earlier historical period
questions.explanation: The functional approach focuses on whether a person can cope with daily life, such as caring for themselves, working and relating to others. Breaking unwritten social rules is the basis of the sociocultural approach.

questions.stem: Left-handed children were once routinely made to write with their right hand at school, but left-handedness is now accepted as normal. Which approach to normality does this change illustrate?
options: Historical
Situational
Statistical
Functional
questions.explanation: The historical approach recognises that what is judged normal changes over time as knowledge and social attitudes change. The proportion of left-handed people has not changed enough to explain the shift, so it is not a statistical judgement.

questions.stem: The situational approach to normality judges behaviour by:
options: whether it was considered acceptable in earlier periods of history
whether it matches the behaviour of most people in the population
whether it is caused by an identifiable physical illness or injury
whether it suits the particular setting in which it occurs
questions.explanation: The situational approach recognises that the same behaviour can be normal in one context and abnormal in another. Whether behaviour was accepted in the past is the historical approach.

questions.stem: Screaming and jumping up and down is seen as normal at a grand final but abnormal in a hospital waiting room. Which approach to normality explains this?
options: Situational
Historical
Medical
Statistical
questions.explanation: The behaviour is the same; only the setting differs, which is the situational approach. The historical approach compares different time periods, not different places at the same time.

questions.stem: The medical approach to normality treats abnormal behaviour as:
options: any behaviour that would have been unusual in a different time period
a symptom of an underlying illness that can be diagnosed and treated
a breach of the rules that a person's cultural group expects them to follow
any behaviour that is shown by only a small percentage of the population
questions.explanation: The medical approach views abnormality as the result of a disorder, often with biological causes, that is identified by its symptoms and treated, for example with medication. Rarity is the statistical approach and breaching cultural rules is the sociocultural approach.

questions.stem: Which is a valid limitation of the medical approach to normality?
options: It can overlook psychological and social causes of behaviour
It cannot be used by doctors because it relies only on cultural norms
It treats all statistically common behaviours as signs of illness
It judges behaviour only by whether it suits the current setting
questions.explanation: By framing abnormal behaviour as illness, the medical approach tends to focus on biological causes and treatments and can neglect factors such as stress, relationships and culture. It is based on symptoms and diagnosis, not on cultural norms, rarity or setting.

questions.stem: A woman cries loudly and wails at her mother's funeral, as is expected in her community. A psychologist unfamiliar with the community judges the behaviour as abnormal because it is unlike what she usually sees. Which two approaches to normality would best show the psychologist's judgement is mistaken?
options: Sociocultural and situational
Statistical and medical
Medical and historical
Statistical and historical
questions.explanation: The behaviour meets the norms of the woman's culture (sociocultural) and suits the setting of a funeral (situational). The psychologist's 'unlike what I usually see' is a statistical judgement, which is exactly what leads to the error.

questions.stem: Why do psychologists usually consider several approaches to normality together rather than relying on one?
options: Each approach has limitations, so together they are more balanced
Each approach gives the same answer, so using several confirms the diagnosis
Only the statistical approach is valid, so the others are used for comparison
Using several approaches removes the need to consider a person's culture
questions.explanation: Each approach captures only part of what makes behaviour normal or abnormal, and each can mislead on its own, for example rare but desirable traits or behaviour that is normal in another culture. Combining them, along with distress and dysfunction, gives a fuller picture.

questions.stem: Ella sleeps about five hours a night, far less than most people her age, yet she feels rested, does well at work and is happy. How would the functional and statistical approaches judge her sleep?
options: Functional: abnormal, because she sleeps too little; statistical: normal, as all sleep varies
Functional: normal, because it suits her job; statistical: normal, because it is common
Functional: normal, because she copes well; statistical: abnormal, because it is uncommon
Functional: abnormal, because it is uncommon; statistical: normal, because she copes well
questions.explanation: The functional approach asks whether behaviour lets a person manage daily life, and Ella functions well. The statistical approach asks only whether behaviour is typical, and very short sleep is uncommon. The two approaches can disagree, which is why neither is used alone.

questions.stem: A psychological disorder is best described as:
options: any behaviour that differs from what most people in a person's age group would do
a physical illness of the brain that can always be seen on a neuroimaging scan
a pattern of thoughts, feelings or behaviour causing significant distress or impairment
any single occasion on which a person feels sad, worried or angry about events in their life
questions.explanation: A psychological disorder involves a clinically significant, persistent disturbance in thinking, emotion or behaviour that causes distress or interferes with daily life. A single episode of sadness or worry is a normal emotional response, and most disorders cannot be diagnosed from a brain scan.

questions.stem: After her dog dies, Ava feels sad and cries often for about a week, then gradually returns to her normal routine. Why would this not be diagnosed as a psychological disorder?
options: Sadness is never a symptom of any psychological disorder in a diagnostic manual
Psychological disorders can be diagnosed only in people who have no stressors
It is statistically rare to feel sad after the death of a much-loved pet
It is a normal, short-lived response that does not impair her functioning
questions.explanation: A disorder involves distress or dysfunction that is significant and persistent, beyond the expected response to an event. Ava's grief is understandable, proportionate and passes. Sadness is a symptom of disorders such as depression, but only when it is severe and lasting.

questions.stem: The DSM-5-TR is published by:
options: the American Medical Association
the American Psychiatric Association
the World Health Organization
the Australian Psychological Society
questions.explanation: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision (2022), is published by the American Psychiatric Association. The ICD-11 is published by the World Health Organization.

questions.stem: How does the scope of the ICD-11 differ from that of the DSM-5-TR?
options: The ICD-11 lists only physical symptoms, while the DSM-5-TR lists only causes
The ICD-11 classifies all diseases and health conditions, not only mental disorders
The ICD-11 classifies only mental disorders, while the DSM-5-TR covers all diseases
The ICD-11 is used only in the United States, while the DSM-5-TR is used worldwide
questions.explanation: The International Classification of Diseases is the World Health Organization's classification of all diseases and health conditions, with a chapter for mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders. The DSM covers only mental disorders.

questions.stem: A government health department wants to compare rates of depression across many countries using a common international coding system. Which manual is it most likely to use, and why?
options: The ICD-11, because it is the World Health Organization's international standard
The DSM-5-TR, because it is the only manual that includes depression as a recognised disorder
The DSM-5-TR, because it is the World Health Organization's standard for health statistics
The ICD-11, because it is the only manual that gives detailed criteria for mental disorders
questions.explanation: The ICD is used around the world by health systems to record and compare diagnoses and causes of death, so it suits international statistics. Both manuals include depression, and the DSM is published by the American Psychiatric Association, not the World Health Organization.

questions.stem: In Australia, a psychiatrist diagnosing a client and a researcher selecting participants with the same disorder often both refer to the DSM-5-TR. Why is it useful for both to use the same manual?
options: It gives everyone the same criteria, so a diagnosis means the same to all
It tells the psychiatrist exactly which medication each client should be given
It removes the need to interview the client or observe their behaviour at all
It guarantees that every diagnosis made with it will be completely accurate
questions.explanation: Shared criteria give a common language, so clinicians can communicate and researchers can be confident their participants have comparable conditions. The manual describes disorders; it does not prescribe treatment, and diagnosis still needs careful clinical assessment.

questions.stem: A diagnostic manual uses a categorical approach. This means that a person is diagnosed with a disorder when they:
options: score on a scale from no symptoms to severe symptoms without any cut-off point
are judged by a clinician to be unusual compared with other members of their culture
show a brain abnormality that matches the description of a disorder in the manual
meet a set number of listed criteria, so the disorder is judged present or absent
questions.explanation: In a categorical system a person either meets the criteria for a disorder or does not. A criticism is that symptoms actually vary by degree, so a person just below the threshold can still be struggling.

questions.stem: Hallucinations, delusions and disorganised speech are characteristic symptoms of which disorder?
options: Schizophrenia
Generalised anxiety disorder
Depression
Antisocial personality disorder
questions.explanation: Schizophrenia, in the category of schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders, involves a loss of contact with reality, shown by hallucinations, delusions and disorganised speech or behaviour. Anxiety disorders involve excessive fear and worry, but the person's contact with reality is intact.

questions.stem: Jordan firmly believes that his neighbours are planting messages in his head through the television, despite clear evidence that this is impossible. This symptom is a:
options: hallucination
phobia
compulsion
delusion
questions.explanation: A delusion is a fixed false belief held despite clear contrary evidence. A hallucination is a false perception, such as hearing voices that are not there, rather than a false belief.

questions.stem: In schizophrenia, a reduction in normal emotional expression and motivation is described as a:
options: positive symptom
delusion
compulsion
negative symptom
questions.explanation: Negative symptoms are the absence or reduction of normal functions, such as flat emotional expression and loss of motivation. Positive symptoms are additions to normal experience, such as hallucinations and delusions; 'positive' does not mean good.

questions.stem: Depression, with persistent low mood and loss of interest or pleasure in usual activities, belongs to which category of psychological disorders?
options: Personality disorders
Schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders
Bipolar and depressive disorders
Anxiety disorders
questions.explanation: Depression is a mood disorder, grouped with bipolar disorder in the category of bipolar and depressive disorders. Anxiety can occur alongside depression, but excessive fear and worry are the core features of anxiety disorders.

questions.stem: How does bipolar disorder differ from depression?
options: Bipolar disorder involves only low mood, while depression involves only high mood
Bipolar disorder is a personality disorder, while depression is an anxiety disorder
Bipolar disorder involves episodes of abnormally elevated mood (mania) as well as low mood
Bipolar disorder involves hallucinations, while depression never involves any changes in mood
questions.explanation: Bipolar disorder is defined by manic or hypomanic episodes of elevated or irritable mood and increased energy, usually alternating with depressive episodes. Depression involves low mood without episodes of mania.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an anxiety disorder?
options: Specific phobia
Antisocial personality disorder
Schizophrenia
Bipolar disorder
questions.explanation: Specific phobia is an anxiety disorder: an intense, irrational and persistent fear of a particular object or situation that leads to avoidance. Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder and bipolar disorder is a mood disorder.

questions.stem: Personality disorders differ from many other psychological disorders because they involve:
options: a long-standing, inflexible pattern of thinking and behaving across situations
a brief episode of symptoms that begins suddenly and usually ends within a few weeks
a loss of contact with reality shown through hallucinations and fixed false beliefs
an intense fear of one specific object or situation that the person avoids
questions.explanation: Personality disorders are enduring patterns of inner experience and behaviour that deviate from cultural expectations, are pervasive and inflexible, and are usually evident from adolescence or early adulthood. A loss of contact with reality describes psychosis.

questions.stem: Over many years, a 30-year-old man has repeatedly lied, broken the law, ignored the safety of others and shown no remorse for hurting people. Which disorder do these features best match?
options: Generalised anxiety disorder
Schizophrenia
Antisocial personality disorder
Specific phobia
questions.explanation: Antisocial personality disorder is a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, including deceitfulness, impulsivity, recklessness and lack of remorse. It is not a psychotic disorder, because the person remains in contact with reality.

questions.stem: Sam has had two episodes of persistent low mood and loss of interest, each lasting several weeks, with months of normal functioning between them. Lee has shown the same rigid distrust of others in every situation since adolescence. Which classification fits best?
options: Sam: schizophrenia spectrum and psychotic disorders; Lee: anxiety disorders
Sam: bipolar and depressive disorders; Lee: personality disorders
Sam: personality disorders; Lee: bipolar and depressive disorders
Sam: anxiety disorders; Lee: schizophrenia spectrum and psychotic disorders
questions.explanation: Episodes of low mood and loss of interest with recovery in between fit a depressive disorder. A pervasive, inflexible pattern present since adolescence and seen across situations is the defining feature of a personality disorder, not an episodic mood problem.

questions.stem: Two psychologists independently assess the same client using the DSM-5-TR and both diagnose generalised anxiety disorder. This agreement indicates:
options: the statistical rarity of the disorder
the cultural fairness of the diagnosis
inter-rater reliability of the diagnosis
predictive validity of the diagnosis
questions.explanation: Reliability in diagnosis is consistency, and inter-rater reliability is the extent to which different clinicians reach the same diagnosis for the same person. Agreement alone does not prove the diagnosis is valid; both could share the same mistaken assumption.

questions.stem: Which situation shows that a diagnosis may be reliable but not valid?
options: One clinician changes a diagnosis after new and more accurate information becomes available
Several clinicians agree on a diagnosis that does not reflect the person's actual condition
Several clinicians disagree on a diagnosis, but each diagnosis predicts the right treatment
One clinician makes a diagnosis that correctly describes the person's actual condition
questions.explanation: Reliability is about consistency, so clinicians can agree consistently and still be wrong, for example if the criteria used do not capture a real, distinct condition. Validity is whether the diagnosis accurately identifies the person's actual condition and predicts its course and treatment.

questions.stem: Why do clear and specific diagnostic criteria tend to improve the reliability of diagnosis?
options: Different clinicians are more likely to interpret the same symptoms in the same way
Clients are less likely to describe their symptoms honestly to the clinician
They guarantee that the diagnosis predicts how the client will respond to treatment
They allow clinicians to rely on their own personal judgement rather than on rules
questions.explanation: Vague criteria leave room for different interpretations, so clinicians disagree; precise criteria make agreement more likely. Reliability does not guarantee validity, so clear criteria alone cannot ensure a diagnosis predicts treatment response.

questions.stem: Many people diagnosed with depression also meet the criteria for an anxiety disorder. Why does this overlap (comorbidity) raise questions about the validity of diagnostic categories?
options: It proves that both depression and anxiety are caused by the same single gene
It shows that the diagnostic manuals list too few symptoms for each disorder
It suggests the categories may not describe truly distinct conditions
It shows that clinicians cannot agree with each other on any diagnosis at all
questions.explanation: If disorders were clearly distinct, they would rarely occur together; frequent overlap suggests the boundaries between categories may be artificial. Comorbidity is a question of validity, not proof that clinicians cannot agree.

questions.stem: A psychologist diagnoses a recently arrived migrant with a disorder after misreading her culturally normal expressions of distress as symptoms. Which issue does this show most clearly?
options: Inter-rater reliability is always low for migrant clients
Statistical rarity is the only valid way to diagnose a disorder
Cultural factors can reduce the validity of a diagnosis
Diagnostic manuals are never used outside the United States
questions.explanation: If a clinician does not understand how distress is expressed in a client's culture, the diagnosis may not reflect the client's actual condition, which is a validity problem. The DSM-5-TR includes guidance on cultural concepts of distress for this reason.

questions.stem: Which is a possible harmful consequence of giving a person a diagnosis of a psychological disorder?
options: The label may lead others to treat the person differently and cause stigma
The label allows the person to access treatment and support services
The label helps the person understand that their symptoms are recognised
The label gives clinicians a shared language for discussing the person's care
questions.explanation: A diagnostic label can lead to stigma and discrimination, and the person may come to see themselves only in terms of the label. Access to treatment, validation and a shared clinical language are benefits of diagnosis, not harms.
